channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: The Australian Landscape
item.description: Traces the knocker's tradition back to the earliest Dutch navigators and British explorers, then through colonial painters and poets who saw the Australian landscape as weird and melancholy, arguing that the mass importation of European animals, plants and aesthetic habits expressed settlers' inability to accept what was already there.

item.title: The Australian Character
item.description: Surveys two centuries of knockers on the Australian national character, from W. G. Grace's disputed 1874 letter savaging colonial cricket fans to Malcolm Muggeridge's lotus-eating portraits and Arthur Koestler's Qantas plastic hook epiphany, tracing also the long shame and eventual pride in the Australian accent.

item.title: The Athletic Passion
item.description: A history of professional pedestrianism and athletics in Australia, from the colonial 'peds' and the great Melbourne-versus-Ireland sprint contests of the 1860s through the careers of Bobby McDonald, Charlie Samuels, Jack Donaldson, Arthur Postle and 'Professor' William Miller, to the Olympic triumphs of Marjorie Jackson, Betty Cuthbert, Herb Elliott and the heartbreaking near-misses of Ron Clarke.

item.title: The Boxing Passion
item.description: Traces the arc of Australian prize fighting from colonial bare-knuckle battles through the careers of Larry Foley, Griffo, Bob Fitzsimmons, Les Darcy and Jack Johnson's stunning defeat of Tommy Burns at Rushcutters Bay in 1908, to the modern champions Jimmy Carruthers, Lionel Rose and Johnny Famechon.

item.title: The Football Passion
item.description: Traces the Australian devotion to Australian Rules football from its 1858 origins at Melbourne Grammar and Scotch College through decades of crowd riots, inter-suburb feuds, the Coleman suspension, the Barassi defection, and the rival passions of Rugby League in New South Wales and Queensland.

item.title: The Gambling Evil
item.description: Traces Australian gambling culture from the colonial era to the 1950s through the saga of John Wren's Collingwood Tote, the anti-gambling crusades of the Reverend Worrall and William Henry Judkins, the flamboyant open-letter war between Judkins and Wren's ally John Norton, the doomed campaigns against starting-price bookmakers, and the long battle of the states over George Adams's Tattersall's lottery before it finally settled in Melbourne in 1954.

item.title: The Evil of Cremation
item.description: Traces Australia's slow, resisted shift from burial to cremation, from Dr Neild's 1873 pitch to the Royal Society and the scandalous 1895 beach cremation of Mrs Henniker at Sandringham, through the founding of Melbourne's Fawkner crematorium in 1927, to the eventual normalisation of cremation across every state.

item.title: The Evil of the Social Evil
item.description: Surveys a century of Australian prostitution euphemised as 'the social evil', from the Theatre Royal's notorious Saddling Paddock and Melbourne's Little Lonsdale Street brothels under Madame Brussels, through the 1891 mystery of Parliament's stolen mace, to Brisbane's condoned, medically inspected brothels and the bikini-era brothel economics of the 1960s.

item.title: The Evil of the Printed Word
item.description: Traces Australia's long, erratic history of literary censorship, from Annie Besant's 1888 birth-control obscenity trial and Professor Marshall Hall's scandalous 1900 dismissal from Melbourne University, through the gaoling of novelist Robert Close in 1948, to the secret Customs blacklist and the eventual 1960s release of Lady Chatterley's Lover and Lolita.

item.title: The Evil of Smoking
item.description: Surveys a century of Australian anti-smoking crusades, from E.W. Cole's illustrated warnings and the Juvenile Smoking Suppression Acts of 1900-1905 to the Methodist church's long, losing battle over whether its own ministers should be allowed to smoke.

item.title: The Theatre Evil and the Evil of Dancing
item.description: Traces the long campaign against theatre-going and dancing as gateways to vice, from Dr Adam Cairns's hellfire 1856 lecture and Bishop Moorhouse's scandalous 1877 invitation of the actor William Creswick to Bishopcourt, through John Alexander Dowie's crusade against 'the terrible trinity of Venus, Bacchus, and the Drama', to the Methodist church's long, losing rearguard action against the dance hall.

item.title: The Evil of Bathing
item.description: Charts a century of council by-laws policing Australian beaches in the name of morality rather than safety, from Sydney's 1833 bathing curfew and W. H. Gocher's defiant 1902 daylight swim at Manly, through Melbourne's sex-segregated Edwardian beaches and the 'no loitering' laws of St Kilda, to the bikini panics of the 1960s.

item.title: The Evil of the Demon Drink
item.description: Traces the colonial appetite for alcohol from Victoria's staggering 1850s statistics, through the failed prohibition experiment at William Chaffey's Mildura irrigation colony, the Blue Ribbon movement and Coffee Palace boom under Premier James Munro, the great barmaid debate and King O'Malley's parliamentary oratory, and on to the six o'clock swill that dominated Australian drinking culture from 1916 to 1966.

item.title: Melbourne
item.description: A portrait of Melbourne in the 1978 anthology, tracing its gold rush bravado, the 1892 bank crash and lasting inferiority complex, Toorak snobbery and the finest buildings, before closing with restaurant recommendations ranging from Emil's in Lonsdale Street to Smacka Fitzgibbon's jazz bar in North Melbourne.

item.title: Melbourne v. Sydney: The Love-Hate Feud
item.description: A Melbourne man's affectionate account of the long civic rivalry between Melbourne and Sydney, from Parliament's original seat in Melbourne to the competing airports, opera houses and sporting loyalties that kept the two cities in a state of permanent, mostly enjoyable mutual suspicion.

item.title: How to Enjoy Hot Christmases
item.description: A defence of the Australian habit of serving roast turkey and plum pudding in midsummer heat, tracing Keith Dunstan's own Melbourne Christmases from the 1880s boom-era house of his childhood to a flying doctor's Christmas at Mt Isa, an Antarctic station's six-bottle dinner, and a Barrier Reef yacht.

item.title: The Humble Uniform
item.description: Traces blue denim from Levi Strauss's 1873 rivet patent with tailor Jacob Davis through Hollywood's James Dean, Marlon Brando and Elvis Presley to the protest fashion of the Vietnam-era counterculture, opening Keith Dunstan's history of Just Jeans with the story of jeans before the company itself existed.

item.title: The Passion at School
item.description: Surveys the near-religious grip of school sport on Australian boarding and grammar schools, from the ritual status of football and rowing colours to the pitched battles between Melbourne Grammar and Wesley College, and closes on the modern anxiety of children's sport turning parents into fanatics.

item.title: The Racing Passion
item.description: Traces Australia's worship of the horse from the colony's first race meetings to the Melbourne Cup, built around three champions the public mourned like royalty, Carbine, Phar Lap and Gunsynd, and the money that racing moves through the nation.

item.title: The Cricket Passion
item.description: Traces cricket's role in binding the Australian colonies into a nation, and the fierce, sometimes poisonous rivalry with England that ran from the first touring elevens through the Sydney riot of 1879, Bradman and Bodyline, to the cancelled 1971-72 South African tour.

item.title: The Swimming Passion
item.description: Traces the rise of Australian swimming from the invention of the crawl and Fanny Durack's fight to compete at the 1912 Olympics, through Andrew 'Boy' Charlton's teenage duel with Arne Borg, to the punishing modern training regimes behind Dawn Fraser, Murray Rose and Shane Gould.

item.title: The Tennis Passion
item.description: Traces Australian tennis from Norman Brookes's penniless 1905 Wimbledon tilt and the Davis Cup mania that followed, through Frank Sedgman and Lew Hoad's fights against professionalism, to Evonne Goolagong's 1971 Wimbledon win over Margaret Court.

item.title: The Rowing Passion
item.description: Traces Australian rowing from Edward Trickett's 1876 world championship and Henry Searle's death and record-breaking funeral, through the Hanlan-Beach sculling rivalry, to Bobby Pearce, Mervyn Wood and the showmanship of Stuart Mackenzie at Henley.

item.title: Printophobia - There's No Known Cure
item.description: A lifelong fear of large print and banner headlines is diagnosed as printophobia, prompting a defence of reading the paper back-to-front, skipping royals, crime and economists, and a closing tally of the truly disastrous Christmases, from the unsolved Bogle murders to Harold Holt's drowning at Portsea, that editors secretly treasure.

item.title: The Deadly Sugar Addiction
item.description: A confession of two decades of sugar and chocolate addiction, from a devotion to fresh liquorice and black jelly beans through the seductive TV advertising of chocolate bars to a subscription to the American magazine Chocolate News, with its profiles of famous chocoholics and reports on chocolate as an Aztec aphrodisiac.

item.title: No Shame for Carnivores
item.description: A return to meat-eating after years of vegetarian, macrobiotic and Pritikin dinner-party fashions, tracing the household's swing from the boneless-lamb TV commercials of the deep-freeze era through a self-conscious vegan and quiche phase back to a butcher offering pre-marinated Mongolian lamb and Hungarian goulash.

item.title: The Confessions of a Coffeeholic
item.description: A defence of coffee addiction runs through a Harvard study that found no link between coffee and heart disease, a history of the drink being banned as satanic or driving men impotent, and famous devotees from Voltaire's 50 cups a day to Fontanelle, who blamed his own 100-year lifespan on the stuff.

item.title: Where Can We Go for Happy Bowel?
item.description: A litany of conflicting food-safety scares, from unprocessed bran turning up laced with pesticide residue and pate riddled with staphylococcus to a Californian friend who travels everywhere with his own BYO bag of bran, ending in despair at whether anything is left safe to eat once mercury in fish and lead in tea are added to the list.

item.title: Manic Cholesterol
item.description: Time magazine's cover story on cholesterol is filed as the latest in a decades-long tradition of manufactured food panics, from a childhood sugar scare that banished Mars Bars for nine months to Reader's Digest's mid-century disease-of-the-week formula, ending in a plea for a single year's amnesty from health scares to enjoy cheese, ham fat and salt in peace.

item.title: Caulie - The Perfect Flower
item.description: A vain streak that once produced giant dahlias named Vivien Leigh and Sammy Davis Jr is redirected into vegetable gardening once nearly everyone in the family's circle turns vegetarian or vegan, ending in a cost analysis showing the home-grown, organic, decidedly average-looking cauliflowers cost four times what the same vegetables would have at the local market.
